The present design therefore reports errors on routine and unusual legitimate activity separately, rather than treating unusualness as proof of misuse.

Valid event losses were averaged within each session, then across sessions in the batch, giving each session equal weight regardless of length. The loss families match categorical, Boolean and continuous temporal targets. Averaging within each family, then across families, avoided giving larger families more weight merely because they contained more encoded dimensions. Each family contributes one third when categorical targets are valid. All approaches used this rule; the study did not test whether it outperformed alternatives.

For each available loss family g, Vᵍᵢₜ is the set of valid targets in family g for event t of session i, and Gᵢₜ contains the families with at least one valid target. Boolean and temporal sets contain three and six outputs, respectively; the categorical set contains the valid fields among thirteen. Tᵢ is the valid session length, and B is the batch of sessions. Batch loss averages the session scores sᵢ, giving each session equal weight regardless of length. All approaches used this rule; alternatives were not compared.

For illustration only, family losses 0.3, 0.3 and 0.6 give event loss 0.4. With no valid categorical targets, Boolean and temporal losses 0.2 and 0.4 give event loss 0.3. An illustrative session with event losses 0.4, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3 and 0.3 has raw score 0.32 and exceeds an illustrative raw threshold of 0.30. Before: Federated learning trains a shared model without pooling raw electronic health record (EHR) access logs, but the server can still inspect individual model updates. This study compared detection performance and training cost with and without secure aggregation of those updates. It evaluated pooled centralised training, standard Federated Averaging and Federated Averaging with Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+) using a long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder, a model that learns to reconstruct routine access sequences. Experiments used one supplied benchmark described as synthetic, three simulated clients and five random seeds. Sampling either retained the original client distributions or favoured selected departments. On the primary test, which included threats, routine access and unusual legitimate activity, the mean paired differences in global average precision, a measure of threat ranking, between SecAgg+ and standard Federated Averaging were +0.0047 and +0.0001 in the two sampling conditions. These differences did not establish equivalent performance. Federated training did not consistently outperform pooled training. Compared with standard Federated Averaging, SecAgg+ increased the time recorded for the training workflow by 132.8% and 128.6%, respectively. The content carried in application messages increased by approximately 49.9%. All configurations struggled with unusual legitimate activity. For SecAgg+, mean false-positive rates were 98.58% and 96.40% on the secondary test, which contained threats and unusual legitimate activity but no routine sessions. Repeating the experiment in a fresh software environment on the same computer reproduced the predictions, with a disclosed difference in stored information about input scaling. Protected aggregation therefore added workflow cost without a clear detection benefit in this benchmark. Protection depended on a trusted host and honest participants. Incomplete records of data generation and the use of simulated clients limit what the findings imply for hospitals.
After: Federated learning trains a shared model without pooling raw electronic health record (EHR) access logs, but the server can still inspect individual model updates. Experiments used one supplied benchmark described as synthetic, three simulated clients and five random seeds. Reference sampling retained the original client distributions; controlled Non-IID sampling favoured selected departments through resampling. On the primary test, which included threats, routine access and unusual legitimate activity, SecAgg+ achieved mean global average precision (AP) of 0.421 and 0.429, respectively. Mean paired AP differences, calculated as SecAgg+ minus standard Federated Averaging, were +0.0047 and +0.0001. These estimates did not establish equivalent performance. Federated training did not consistently outperform pooled training. Relative to standard Federated Averaging, SecAgg+ increased recorded training-workflow time by 132.8% and 128.6%, and application-message content by approximately 49.9%. All configurations struggled with unusual legitimate activity. SecAgg+ had mean false-positive rates of 98.58% and 96.40% on the secondary test, which contained threats and unusual legitimate activity without routine sessions. A fresh-environment replay on the same computer reproduced the predictions, with a disclosed input-scaling metadata exception. The comparison quantifies the workflow cost of masking updates and identifies persistent false alerts on legitimate exceptions. Protection depended on a trusted host and honest participants. Incomplete data-generation records and simulated clients limit implications for hospitals.
